*By CNN Staff*

CAMBRIDGE, England — Stephen Hawking, the celebrated theoretical physicist whose groundbreaking work on black holes and the origins of the universe made him one of the most recognizable scientists of the modern era, has been hospitalized, Cambridge University confirmed Wednesday.

Details surrounding Hawking's condition remain limited, but a university spokesperson said he is receiving care and that his family has requested privacy during this time.

"Professor Hawking is currently receiving medical attention. We ask that the public respect the family's wishes for privacy as they navigate this difficult period," the university statement read. **A Towering Intellectual Legacy**

Hawking, 76, has long been regarded as one of the most brilliant minds in modern science. A professor at Cambridge University for much of his career, he rose to international prominence with his research on black holes, cosmology, and the nature of space and time. His 1988 book, "A Brief History of Time," became a global bestseller, translated into more than 35 languages and selling over 10 million copies, introducing complex scientific concepts to a mainstream audience in accessible terms.

His contributions to theoretical physics, including what is now known as "Hawking radiation" — the theoretical prediction that black holes emit radiation and can eventually evaporate — reshaped scientific understanding of the cosmos and cemented his status as one of the preeminent physicists since Einstein.

**Living with ALS for Over Five Decades**

Hawking's personal story has been as remarkable as his scientific achievements. In 1963, at just 21 years old, he was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a progressive neurodegenerative disease that attacks nerve cells controlling voluntary muscle movement. Doctors at the time gave him only a few years to live.

Defying those grim predictions, Hawking continued his academic work for decades, even as the disease gradually robbed him of his physical abilities. By the mid-1980s, he had lost the ability to speak naturally following a tracheotomy, and he became reliant on a wheelchair for mobility. He famously communicated through a speech-generating device controlled initially by hand and later by movements of his cheek muscle, allowing him to continue lecturing, writing, and engaging with the public despite his physical limitations.

Hawking's resilience in the face of his diagnosis became almost as celebrated as his scientific discoveries, inspiring millions around the world and raising awareness about ALS and disability.

**A Life of Recognition**

Over his career, Hawking received numerous accolades, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the Copley Medal, and the Fundamental Physics Prize. He held the position of Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge — a position once held by Sir Isaac Newton — for 30 years.

Colleagues and admirers have often pointed not only to his scientific contributions but to his enduring wit, resilience, and commitment to public science communication.

As of Wednesday evening, further updates on Hawking's condition were not immediately available. CNN will continue to follow this developing story.
